family_lesson.where_to_look_first: Go to the flower: local Aristolochia has a single petaloid fused perianth/calyx tube, often bent or inflated, with no ordinary separate petal whorl. Then confirm alternate simple often cordate/palmately veined leaves, an inferior ovary, anthers associated with the stylar column/gynostemium and a many-seeded capsule.
authoritative_framework: Leaves alternate, simple, often cordate/palmately veined and exstipulate, though pseudostipules may occur.
Flowers are bisexual and commonly strongly zygomorphic in Aristolochia.
The conspicuous petaloid structure is a fused perianth/calyx; petals are absent in Aristolochia.
Ovary is inferior in the common Aristolochia framework.
Stamens/anthers are closely associated with or adnate to the stylar column.
Fruit is commonly a many-seeded capsule.
avoid_overgeneralizing: Do not call the showy Aristolochia perianth a corolla of ordinary petals.
Do not use vine habit as mandatory; Aristolochia erecta is an erect perennial.
Do not identify the family from cordate leaves alone.
Do not require a huge Dutchman's-pipe flower; local A. erecta is much smaller.

confusable_families.Apocynaceae: Apocynaceae commonly has a true fused corolla and superior ovary; local Aristolochia has a petaloid fused calyx/perianth, no normal corolla, and inferior ovary.
confusable_families.Convolvulaceae: Morning-glories have a plicate fused corolla and superior ovary/capsule; Aristolochia has the distinctive single petaloid perianth tube and inferior ovary.
